item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q018_tal_effector_repeat_lengths","answer":"d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, and d4cj9a_ are all classified in SCOPe family a.298.1.1 because the classified unit is the homologous TAL-effector repeat array/scaffold, not a fixed-length globular domain. TAL effectors are all-alpha repeat proteins: each repeat is a similar helix-turn-helix-like module, usually about 33-35 residues, and natural or engineered proteins contain different numbers of these repeats. Thus their total SCOPe domain lengths can differ greatly while the underlying repeat architecture, ancestry, and fold remain the same.\n\nAt the hierarchy level, a.298 is the TAL-effector fold, a.298.1 is the TAL-effector superfamily, and a.298.1.1 is the TAL-effector family. The family assignment supports homology of the repeat scaffold among these domains, but it does not mean the proteins have comparable full-length sequences, identical repeat counts, identical DNA targets, or interchangeable biological specificity. In particular, the repeat-variable diresidues that determine base preference can differ, so DNA-binding specificity should not be transferred merely from family membership. For template use, one can transfer the general TAL repeat-array geometry and repeat-level alignment, but not assume a single global alignment, matching domain length, or equivalent target recognition across d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, and d4cj9a_. Representative selection should therefore account for repeat number and target-specific RVD composition, not just the shared SCOPe family label.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
